candidates.text: Raw Materials: Studio Lenca - A Place Within Me For Salvadoran artist Studio Lenca – aka José Campos – El Salvador exists somewhere between memory and imagination. A place carried across distance, remembered through gestures and landscapes, and through the feeling of a home that was never entirely his to inhabit. Raised in the U.S., where his family lived as ‘illegal aliens’ after their displacement during the Salvadoran Civil War, Campos now uses his practice to reclaim autonomy over a fragmented history, merging biographical anecdotes, personal reflections, and folkloric iconography that unpack his own sense of belonging. - Meme Flores Returning to El Salvador in 2025 while developing work for his exhibition COSITAS, Campos connects with filmmaker and cinematographer Meme Flores to document his journey for the short film Studio Lenca - A Place Within Me . Shot on 16mm film between Castillo Venturoso and Campos’ hometown of Santiago Nonualco, the film grew through encounters with the landscapes, people and traditions that inform his relationship with El Salvador, from the Historiantes – traditional dancers who serve as a key reference in his art – to the distinct colors, sounds, and light that shape the environment. Finding a space where the familiar becomes slightly strange, Flores molds a quiet observation of the place we carry long after we have left it, stepping into Campos’ vision of El Salvador as somewhere held between closeness and distance.

candidates.text: Private View: ​Stefan Brüggemann: In No Time Based between London, Mexico City and Ibiza, Mexican conceptual artist Stefan Brüggemann unpacks the philosophy of language in text-driven works that carry acerbic or timely messages. Embedding social criticism in dynamic spray-painted or gold-leafed canvases, neon lights, and large-scale installations, Brüggemann’s work exists at the intersection of punk and refinement, intentionally disrupting the grandeur projected by his raw materials. Directed by Giacomo Gex and voiced by Iggy Pop, the short documentary Stefan Brüggemann: In No Time captures the artist through the faith and philosophy that drives him creatively, in a poetic reflection on the passing of time. - Stefan Brüggemann In Ibiza, Brüggemann’s studio-cum-residence has become a space for inspiration and recalibration, grounded in the island’s contrasts – reinforcing the artistic juxtapositions that sustain his practice. Staging interventions that inhabit the architecture and the surrounding environment, the film frames Stefan’s house and garden as a living artwork, with the island itself as a key character – shot between 16mm film, 8mm film, MiniDV tape and digital formats to document the calm and chaos of the landscape, and its distinctive color palette across the seasons.

candidates.text: Raw Materials: Diego Delgado-Elias Drawn to historic buildings and the traces they carry, Peruvian designer and architect Diego Delgado-Elias has spent his 20-year career reinforcing the elements that develop a space’s warmth and character. Based in Paris, his architecture and interior design studio expands this affinity for creating lived-in spaces that seem to have accumulated naturally over time, observing the lives that occupied a house before him – left as marks on walls, layers of paint, or objects that appear frozen and unmoved. - Daniel Guix While working to restore a seventeenth-century house in the Provençal village of Visan, France, Delgado-Elias found a place that quietly mirrors his sentimental understanding and way of looking at spaces. Moving between past and present, the house becomes an echo of other spaces and sensations that remain with him, while bearing the influence of the surrounding nature in its preserved frescoes, original materials, and domestic objects. For a new short documentary, director Daniel Guix studies Delgado-Elias’ world through the house, exploring how our earliest encounters with spaces can mold our sensibility. Shooting on 16mm, to capture the grain, movement and texture of memory, Guix brings Delgado-Elias’ reflections into conversation with the house, as a rhythm that connects one room to the next, and a reminder of the formative impressions that unconsciously shape creative vision.

candidates.text: In On Rape and Institutional Failure, an exhibition centered on the second chapter of her ongoing project A History of Misogyny, Laia Abril examines different forms of violence against women throughout history.Weaving together images, compiled testimonies, archival materials, select objects, and installations with sound and video, the exhibition investigates how gender-based stereotypes, coupled with worldwide prejudices and misconceptions, have contributed to a systemic rape culture that persists today. By focusing on institutions, Abril aims to avoid narratives of victim-blaming, instead addressing the on-going problem of social accountability that has allowed offenders and enablers alike to avoid justice. On Rape and Institutional Failure was first exhibited in 2020 in the wake of the initial, galvanizing allegations against Harvey Weinstein and other powerful men. While #MeToo has led to few sustained consequences and little systemic change, Abril offers a meaningful opportunity to address the long history of silencing victims and the transgenerational trauma that has developed as a result. She is also the Managing Director for Women Photograph and co-editor of the book Women Photograph: What We See. Previously, she worked as Curatorial Assistant and Collections Manager at the Smithsonian’s National Portrait Gallery. Sara holds an MA in Art History from NYU’s Institute of Fine Arts.
